text: This is Munim: a household shopping agent you fund privately, in shielded Zcash.
A funder sends TAZ to the purse. The spending cap rides inside the encrypted memo: three hundred rupees.
On the public explorer the transaction is shielded. No amount, no memo, nothing to read.
Munim is an installable web app. On the phone, Chrome installs it like any other app.
No app store, no terminal. The household runs it from the home screen.
The deposit is already on the timeline, decrypted by the purse. Cap three hundred, with three eighty-nine rupees available.
Rules say what to buy, and when.
This one buys a two-fifty Swiggy Money card when I say top-up. Fire now, and the agent goes to work.
Thirty seconds later the card is bought on Bitrefill and delivered. Available drops to one thirty-nine.
A Dubai trip in my calendar became an eSIM proposal by itself. It buys only after I approve.

The purse page shows the cap, the spend and every deposit. And the Swiggy Money card: the top-up was redeemed into the household balance automatically, the same balance that paid for last night's Instamart order.

Every purchase sends a receipt back to the funder as an encrypted memo, with a hash of the gift-card code, never the code itself. Paste a receipt into the verifier and it checks the invoice against Bitrefill.
Connections shows every link Munim has: Swiggy's official MCP, Bitrefill, Google Calendar, the wallets. And push notifications, straight to the phone.
There it is, right next to Swiggy's own message confirming the two-fifty credit.
The privacy page says what each party can see, and what they cannot.
Munim is open source under MIT, built for the Free Society Hack. Fund it privately. It shops while you sleep.
